title: Steve Gunn - Breaking and Entering
transcript:
American singer-songwriter and guitarist Steve Gunn spoke with Lauren Taylor by phone from Sydney on 6 July 2017, during his Australian tour. The former member of Kurt Vile's backing band The Violators was introduced with an estimated thirteen albums since 2007, six of them solo, including Eyes on the Lines. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: You're in Sydney for your show tonight. You're an avid record collector, a 'deep music appreciator and a record nerd', to quote you. Are there plans to set aside time to visit record stores while you're in Australia?

Steve: Yeah, I hope so. That's always on the agenda. When I have free time, that's sort of the first thing I look for. I got here yesterday and haven't had all that much time, but I'm hoping there's a window at least later today or definitely tomorrow that I can look around.

Lauren: We've got some fantastic record stores in Melbourne, so here's hoping you find some gold to take home. Is there anything in particular you search for when you go digging?

Steve: I usually kind of gravitate towards used records, the records that have recently arrived. I have a joke with my band that we're always racing to the new arrivals because usually those are the best ones, maybe a first-come, first-served kind of thing. I have pretty broad taste, whether it's jazz, rock or odd odds and ends, a pretty eclectic taste. I kind of look through everything, I suppose.

Lauren: You grew up in record stores in Philadelphia. I loved discovering that the first cassettes you bought were Misfits and Metallica, and you started playing in a hardcore band as a teenager. The music you're making is very different now, but do you still listen to that more aggressive music?

Steve: Yeah, I do. I go through phases of bands and revisit their catalogue a bit. I certainly like to revisit that stuff a lot and still look out for those kinds of records, for sure.

Lauren: Were you always musical from a young age? Do you remember what made you want to pick up the guitar?

Steve: Yeah, I think my parents are pretty musical, and they were always listening to music in the house. I had an older sister. I know a lot of people who started bands always have an older sibling who was an influence. My older sister was really into music, and I thought she was the coolest person. I started emulating her and her friends, and a lot of her friends were in bands. That was enough for me to want to play guitar.

Lauren: You're a prolific artist in terms of your musical output. Is it important creatively to keep things moving?

Steve: Yeah, I think so. I like to cycle through ideas and move along through records and keep the wheels turning. I think a lot of the music and some of the guitar playing I still do is somewhat improvised and spontaneous. I like to keep that element to the music and just roll through. Of course I play older songs, but I'm always working.

Lauren: You worked with Kurt Vile as a member of The Violators. You've said you've been inspired by his ability to make songs sound effortless but also powerful. Is that important for you to achieve with your own music, and how difficult is it?

Steve: I think it's harder for me. I can't just pull a song out of my head immediately. I try, but for me it's a longer process. I think I'm learning the process still, letting my guard down a bit and letting songwriting take over. It's something I've learned to do, and it's not easy. There's a certain sense of letting go and letting your mind take over. Certain people have that ability. Kurt does, and I find that inspiring.

Lauren: You've said your songs aren't necessarily about yourself, that you try to keep away from personal or confessional lyrics and are more inspired by other people's stories and characters, real or fictional. I read about a study suggesting that fiction can increase empathy towards people perceived as outsiders, and the more absorbed readers were in the story, the more empathetically they behaved. What draws you towards other people's stories? Do you find comfort in storytelling?

Steve: I do, and I'm really interested in storytelling. I feel like there's a focus in the public on people who are waving their arms and screaming for it. I appreciate the more subtle stories in the world and people who are perhaps in the shadows or on the fringes of the peripheral public view, if you will. I think the most interesting stories are often untold and sitting right in front of you. You just have to have that openness and the way to observe your surroundings and appreciate some of the people that a lot of people are passing by and uninterested in. That's one thing I'm very interested in.

Lauren: Is there comfort in storytelling as a form of escapism?

Steve: Yeah, certainly. For me, it's a way of escaping. It's a way to use poetic language and descriptive language and set a tone and a story. I really like to work with creating a visual kind of atmosphere and let people take the songs and interpret them, perhaps in a way I hadn't intended, but hopefully it's still positive. It's interesting to talk to people and see how they interpret some of the songs.

Lauren: Have there been interesting interpretations that have taken you aback?

Steve: Yeah. Some songs kind of come to me and almost have a silly storyline. Perhaps it's just a neighbour that's bothering me, and I write this song as a letter to that neighbour. That's not explicit in the story, but when some people hear the song, they think it's about something more worldly and on a bigger scale, which I like.

Lauren: With your songs mainly focused on other people rather than yourself, was it a difficult adjustment from being part of a backing band to stepping out as the front person, with the attention on you? Was it hard to let your guard down?

Steve: I wouldn't call it hard. It was just a different sort of thing, a different way and sensibility, and a lot more questions about who I was. I had to step up and get behind the music and explain myself a bit more, which wasn't something I was used to. But I'm certainly really grateful to anyone who wants to talk to me about my music, and I've learned to let my guard down and speak openly about it.

Lauren: We were chatting about letting go. One of the themes in Eyes on the Lines seems to be characters getting lost and trying to find their way home, or it seems unclear where they're headed. I understand Rebecca Solnit's A Field Guide to Getting Lost had a big impact on you. There's a quote from the book: 'Never to get lost is not to live.' How important is embracing mystery and leaving the door open to the unknown in life?

Steve: Yeah, I think on a broader scheme that kind of sensibility is really getting lost, no pun intended. For me, I think it's important to trust yourself and your instincts, whether you're an artist or pursuing life in a different medium, even if you're just walking down the street. You have to leave a certain part of your perspective open to that. For me, that's where the most interesting experiences lie, where you're not navigating and knowing exactly where you're going to go. Perhaps you'll discover something or bump into someone or learn something. I feel like Rebecca Solnit captures an interesting perspective on holding on to that and incorporating it into your life. I certainly approach music in that way, and also everyday life. I try to keep that perspective. I feel it's something valuable to pursue, especially in these times.

Lauren: I find that idea of being lost as being fully present interesting, not getting caught up in how you think things are meant to be. But it's not easy to surrender to what is, is it?

Steve: For me, I can compare it to improvising as a musician. If you're playing with someone else or by yourself, you let yourself go a little bit and see where it takes you. I think that can be said for a lot of things in life. A lot of people are always panicked about not knowing where they're going to go or what's going to happen. I feel like there's a lot of stress and worry about those things. If you have the right perspective, I think you can just trust the process of what you're doing.

Lauren: The title Eyes on the Lines can have multiple meanings: horizon lines, guitar lines, highway lines. Can you tell us about the concept behind it?

Steve: Sure. I think, for me, music serves as a kind of meditation device. I always get questions about these very cyclical, rhythmic, repetitive songs. They're that way for a reason. I really gravitate towards meditative music. Part of the idea for the title was travelling and focusing your eyes on perhaps passing landscapes, but as you're doing that, you're thinking about other things. I did a lot of that the past few years as I've been touring around. I felt like the title represents a few different things. It represents that action. I also felt a lot of inspiration from a certain group of artists who were studying minimalism, working with lines and the process of their artwork, in whatever medium, and really focusing on this meditative process. That's important to what I do, and I felt like the title represented that as a whole.

Lauren: It's been lovely chatting with you. The NGV Friday night show is sold out, but you're also at the Northcote Social Club on Saturday, July eighth, with Jess Ribeiro and Andrew Tuttle. All the best for those shows and your Australian tour, including Sydney tonight. We're going to finish with 'Ancient Jules'. Were there key characters who guided you with this one? How did the narrative take shape?

Steve: Yeah, there was someone in New York City who inspired this idea for the song. It was a guy I randomly met, a really mystic character, an older guy. I realised he had all these incredible stories. I met him by chance, and he became a friend of mine. He's still around, this incredible old guy who's seen it all, and I didn't know that until we were able to hang out. He would invite me over to his place, play me music, and we'd talk. That's sort of a dedication to him.

Lauren: Thank you so much for joining me on Breaking and Entering today.

Steve: Thank you.
